If he has already appeared in this case as a witness, perhaps you should take his story as the official one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document, that's D157. Based upon your military experience, or years as a general, what do you say about -- or what should Mr. Halilovic's response have been to this order, if it had been issued by Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a number of difficulties with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: First is the hypothetical one, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The second is that -- as I've indicated the defence impugns this document notwithstanding that we tendered it. We tendered it with warts and all and we propose to raise that at all times but I'm -- anyway, I've made my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Based upon your military expertise and experience, what is the response that a -- what is the correct response from a commander to receiving an order in these terms? In military terms what should a commander do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, there is another matter that has to be raised here. This is directed to two commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, whichever one it's directed to, it's -- it's a question the witness can surely answer as a retired general in the army, what you should do if you get an order like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this is a general question. Let the witness answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour could I just explain what it is that I'm concerned about? There are a number of different instructions there and they may or may not be directed to the same person. In other words, it may be or it may not be that the Chief of Staff of the SVK was required to comply with all three. It may be that the commander of the 6th Corps was required to comply with one or others. It may be that the answer is able to be given, maybe it's not, but it has to be clear, though. When my friend puts that thing, "What should a commander do," when it's directed to two commanders that issue has to be addressed. It can't be just put as a hypothetical for one commander because it's not addressed to one commander. It's addressed to two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecution is asking a general question, in the general circumstances, what should a commander do rather than concentrating on this specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If the general question is not attaching to the order, then I've got no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it is attaching to this type of document, of course it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. At first I believe that you have to ask a general question. Then, if necessary, let's come to the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm just looking for the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question was based upon your military expertise and experience, what would the correct response from a commander be to receiving an order in the terms of this particular document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each commander at any level of command, generally speaking, whether receiving an order from a superior officer, and even if this is not the case, if no order is received from a superior, if there is information that comes in from his subordinates or in a different way, indicating that some units have perpetrated a certain type of crime, criminal offence, first and foremost, this commander must ensure that some sort of initial briefing takes place involving the commanders of the subordinate units. At this initial briefing, the unit commanders would be expected to report on the issue in hand, depending on how much information is obtained by the commander from his subordinate commanders in relation to a given crime, if that's what we are talking about. Depending on whether information is satisfactory in terms of scope and in terms of depth, the commander must then proceed and request his commander for security to immediately initiate an investigation to set up a working relationship with the civilian police, and to have a joint investigation. That would be necessary. Then automatically, the security service must initiate criminal proceedings. This would be all that a commander would be expected and obliged to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the lines, "Isolate the perpetrators and take energetic measures"? How would a commander be expected -- or what steps should a commander take to quote "isolate the perpetrators and take energetic measures"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I just raise a matter there. It has to be clear whether this is a general question or whether he's being asked what steps should General Halilovic have taken or Salko Gusic have taken in this situation because the difference between a theoretical approach and what should have happened in the real case must be drawn, and I made this objection before so that has to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this time I would not say what is my understanding. I would let Mr. Re to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's actually a general question but it leads to the same result. I mean, the question of material ability is of legal submission at the end of the day, but the theoretical is certainly a general and a practical one, but it's a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If it's a general question, let's stick to it. Just, you know -- ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's certainly a general question, General.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, the unit commander, and I'm picking up where I left off, following a briefing with his subordinate unit commanders, after it has been ascertained that a crime occurred, at this point the unit commander should make a decision as to what to do now. The investigation must get off the ground immediately. It must be initiated by the security service, as I was saying. However, I'm trying to say this: It's down to the commander entirely to decide whether combat operations should continue or cease. In order for combat operations to cease, he must first obtain approval from his superior officer, needless to say. The commanders' mission as it pertains to a given combat task or operation always comes first. If an operation cannot be stopped, or, rather, an operation cannot be stopped simply because an individual, civilian or not, has been killed, or five individuals, or ten individuals, if we are looking at a large scale operation or mission. The mission or the operation must go on until all the tasks are completed. However, once it has been ascertained that a crime has occurred, this should by no means stop the security service from prosecuting any crime that has occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What role does the commander have -- sorry, if I've interrupted you, please continue.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are speaking in very general terms. But this very much depends on the nature of the crime that has occurred and its scope. The commander should accordingly take measures to put things under control, to reassert control over what's going on, to stop the crime from spreading or from recurring. He should isolate perpetrators. But then most of this is down to the security service having first obtained approval from the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is the security service obliged or expected to report back the results of their investigations to the commander who has ordered them to conduct the investigations?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very complex question. Can you please repeat it? It's a very serious question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The commander you've ordered an investigation, having been informed of a crime -- I'm sorry, you've asked the security service to investigate something and they go off and do it, is the chief of the security service or whoever you've delegated it to obliged to report back to you as a commander at the conclusion of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is somewhat difficult. The reason is I'm not certain that I have a full mastery of the book of rules applied by the security service. What their authorities are, what their powers are, what their tasks are, and what measures they are authorised to take. And that's why I'm saying that this question requires a very thorough expert examination. However, it would only be natural for the security service from the same command, the commander's security service, to report back to him. Nevertheless, in practice, and I believe this must be enshrined in the rules governing the work of the security service, no matter what the case was, the security bodies would always send their reports to their own superior in the security service itself, and they would inform their commander to the extent previously authorised by their own superior within the security service, if you get my meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P124?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 15th of September 1993, headed "order," with the name Sefer Halilovic at the bottom of it and a signature over the name, addressed to 317th Brigade commander, the 45th Brigade commander and the Prozor Independent Battalion commander. I just want you to look at that document. When did you first see that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw it after I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From your experience as a very senior, retired general, what can you say about the type of order that that is?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of its substance, it's much like one of the documents that we looked at, the one that involves Zulfikar, except this does not say, "Order for attack." But this kind of document talks about how to organise a combat means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you -- can you comment upon the level of detail in this particular order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very least, I should go through the document thoroughly, compare it to a military map, and then I could say something. This is a very brief order that has to do with combat resources. It may or may not be consistent with other, more thorough and more comprehensive documents or it may stand on its own. If you look at the document, you see that there is a list of tasks that were given to various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to give you the opportunity to look at a map, which is D131. I'll ask you about the map, then I'll return to the document when you've commented on the map. When was the first time you saw that particular map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, I want you to comment upon the format of this particular map, in terms of -- what I have here is just an identical copy for my own purposes, so don't worry about this one here. Look at the coloured one behind you, to your right. I want you to comment upon the map and the format of the map. In military terms, in the Bosnian army, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I only saw the copy of this map last week, and this is the first time I've laid eyes on the original. It's a topographic map to show how any type of combat operations were planned, specifically the case before us is the Neretva operation. I can simply state that this is the usual type of topographic map with the Neretva operation plan marked on it. It contains all the basic and crucial details that a map like this should show, or an operation plan like this, when it's shown on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. There are signatures on the map, or there are names on the map. On the top left-hand of the map is Rasim Delic's and on the bottom right, Sefer Halilovic's. What can you say about the positioning of Rasim Delic's at the top left and Sefer Halilovic's at the bottom right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two options. If you have a plan like this marked on a map for a particular type of combat operations by a particular command, regardless of the specific level of this command, then in the lower right-hand corner, you should have the name of the Chief of Staff if it's a comprehensive operation. This operation plan or combat operation plan would normally be produced by a staff at any level in the chain of command, and the upper left-hand corner you should have the first and last name of the commander of the unit approving the plan, this combat operation plan. The other option is there is a subordinate unit or subordinate command drawing up a plan like this and marking it on a map. And quite specifically, if this is drafted by the corps, as I did a great many times, then my signature would be where Sefer Halilovic's signature is, as the commander of the 1st Corps, in which capacity I have drafted plans and maps like this. And then in the upper left-hand corner, you would have the name of my superior commander, Rasim Delic, followed by his rank and specific position, because he is in this case the one who approves the plan. This one specifically was produced by the Supreme Command Staff, and, sure enough, this map meets the fundamental requirements applied when a plan or a topographic map like there is produced. It does have a number of minor faults which are of no consequence. Up there it says Neretva operation, and the next thing that should be marked is the type of map, the scale, the time when the operation is due to commence, and that sort of information, but these are minor details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From looking at this map, can you say who was in command and control of combat?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That too is a complex question. It is obvious on the map that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, Sefer Halilovic, authored the map, or rather his officers drafted the map. Or, rather, his staff did. Naturally, by his signature, he stands by the map on behalf of his staff and to corroborate and confirm this decision. In the upper corner you can see that it has been approved by the commander, which means that the Supreme Command Staff is actually the body that drafted this decision. However, I also have to give you at least two possible variants that might occur. The first variant or possibility is that Chief of Staff drafted this decision, the commander approved the decision, and the Chief of Staff then was charged with personally being in charge of control and command, in terms of the execution of this particular plan of operations. Then again, there could have been a second variant. Namely, the Chief of Staff with his staff drafted this plan of operations on orders from the commander. The commander approved it, and as to the question of who will be the chief officer in command, who will be in command, which of course is not that often the case, can be the kind of question that would be dealt with subsequently, after the actual production of such a plan of operations. Let me remark that along with a topographic map of this kind which has drawn into it the plan -- the plan of operations, must necessarily be accompanied by a combat order, written, the text of the combat order, for the actual execution of the operation in question. In its full scope an operation of this kind, which is quite complex operation, should be accompanied by a written document of at least 50 or up to 100 pages, including the orders for all the arms of service, and the combat orders for all the participants in the execution of such a plan of operations. What specifically is the situation here is something that I cannot say because I would require more time for that in order to study many more documents which pertain to this, especially many more documents. In relation to the number of documents that I've already had occasion to examine, I would also have to study numerous legal regulations. I would have to speak to a much larger number of people and so on and so forth. Namely this, as I've already mentioned, requires an expert approach in order for me to be able to give you a more comprehensive reply in the sense of an answer to the question whether General Sefer Halilovic was the sole and genuine commander of this operation or not. Or perhaps things evolved somewhat differently. Perhaps somewhere midway between these two solutions or variants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we -- can you please return to the document on the screen, P124? I think before I showed you the map you said you wanted to see a map. Yes. You said "at the very least I should go through the document thoroughly, compare it to a military map, then I could say something." Now, what I want you to do is go through the document and compare it to that military map and then say something. What I want to know is whether that order, P124, relates to what you see on the map, D131, based upon your extensive military experience and your retiring last year as a general in the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now I do object. Your Honours, what the Prosecutor has asked here, I must be very precise about it, he's asked him to go through that document and compare it to that military map. "What I want to know," said Mr. Re, "is whether that order, P124, relates to what you see and the map, D131." Now, Your Honours were present -- of course, necessarily present whether I made the same point when my learned friend Ms. Chana was taking a witness. It's just playing a -- I can't think of a better term, than this, playing a card trick with the witness. To get the witness to pick out that order which we know about and not to refer to the other orders that relate to the particular episode at Uzdol, which we also know about, in my submission, is very misleading and very unfair to the witness. When I say misleading, I don't mean to cast personal aspersion. I just mean it puts the witness in a position of having to give an opinion based on little knowledge. So I object to this question being asked in relation to this document, unless it be shown that the witness has got -- has at least been acquainted with the relevant other documents that concern that particular axis of attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To my understanding, that's -- document P124, as well as the map, D131, are already admitted into the evidence already. This witness gives testimony to those two documents, and he said that he never seen those two documents before he came to The Hague. So I wonder how much we could get from the testimony of this witness, whether his testimony will be any assistance to our case. Because I understand that this witness is called as a fact witness, not as an expert witness, in our particular case. Mr. Re, I hone you could take my remarks into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly do, but I certainly note that each of the military people we've -- senior military people we have called have been cross-examined at some length about matters that are basically of expertise, asked to comment upon subordination, documents, what they mean militarily, and I anticipate, and I hope I won't be disappointed because I anticipate Mr. Morrissey will do exactly the same with this witness. And what I'm asking is the retired general to comment, because his units were involved in these particular operations, in what these documents mean. It may obviate the need for us to call expert evidence if he can give an opinion based upon his expertise of what they mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this situation, you might ask some questions related to the unit attached to this witness's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This particular order doesn't refer to the 9th or the 10th Brigade specifically, but the question I'm after is -- the answer -- what I want to ask him about is the meaning of resubordination there in terms of the document, and relating that to the map which the witness asked to -- we asked to see a military map. That's why I showed him the map. And I asked him to comment in general terms upon the detail there. He said he would need to look at a map. I was going to ask him how it that relates to the map which is the map in question and about the resubordination and how it relates to the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, the witness testified he never saw these two documents before he came to The Hague. How could he give some reliable testimony on the resubordination issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That didn't stop the Defence asking Mr. Gusic about the inspection team order, for example, and he hadn't seen that either. I mean, every witness who is of a certain level has been asked to comment upon the meaning of something, and I will ask Mr. Karavelic about the inspection team; I'm sure Mr. Morrissey will do exactly the same and put his case to the witness because the witness is a general. He will ask him what an inspection team is, and what this means, and what Mr. Halilovic really in command or control or was it a coordinating role? These questions have been asked of everyone. They will be asked of this witness by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the inspection team, I believe there is some reasons and grounds for putting some questions to this witness, of course, on the basis to know whether this witness is aware of that inspection team or not. But as for this map, and the document, I have serious doubts about that. In the meantime, the Defence has the objections to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next document. I withdraw that. I want to move now to the return of the 9th and the 10th Brigade to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say now: How long after they left that they actually returned to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with precision when they returned. I believe that there is a report on when the 2nd Independent Battalion or some of the units of the 2nd Independent Battalion returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the 9th and the 10th? Are you able to say in days or weeks how long after they left did they actually return to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that they did not return within the scheduled time according to my orders. They stayed much longer. But I would have to track down the pertinent documents to check on the exact dates of their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you referring to a period of seven days there, are you? That's scheduled time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I'm referring to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Upon their return, did you have communication with Mr. Halilovic in relation to these units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document 65 ter 77, which is number RR271562?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 389.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have the document there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's an order of the 23rd of September 1993 from the name at the bottom is Sefer Halilovic with a signature over it addressed to the 1st Corps commander, 1st Corps command, I'm sorry, to the attention of the commander. The order has number 02/1109-1. Now, is this an order that Mr. Halilovic sent to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this document, that's it. I think this is what I referred to the day -- yesterday or the day before yesterday, when I said that an order had arrived asking for units. They did not designate specifically what units but just a number of units that were required with a specific number of men per unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember actually speaking to Mr. Halilovic in relation to this order, either before or after you received it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any specific conversation or any element from any such conversations. In fact I think that we did talk about it but I cannot recall any details of such conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your personal reaction to receiving an order asking for more soldiers from Mr. Halilovic? Not your response, but your personal reaction.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do when you received this order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was I supposed to do? I acted accordingly. I obeyed the order. I proceeded to set up this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you obtain the -- the soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be other documents, follow-up documents, to this order. I believe I tried to establish a battalion using three or four from other brigades. I assigned Zijo Rujanac as commander and his deputy was supposed to be Fuad Abadzic. There was a certain amount of trouble with these two men, and I believe I then issued another document appointing different people instead of those two, and so on and so forth. And unless I'm mistaken, this unit never left due to some difficulties. And then soon after, the Neretva operation was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Point 4 of the order says "The battalion commander will lead the unit from Sarajevo at 1900 hours on the 23rd of September 1993, transport from Hrasnica is organised in a motorised vehicle, direction of march, Sarajevo, Hrasnica, Pazaric, Bradina, Neretva River, Donja Jablanica. Commander of the unit will in Donja Jablanica report within the unit OSVKIKM," [sic] that's the Supreme Staff command forward command post. Why have you said there that they should report to the Supreme Command Staff forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you expect me to tell you, because everything was an option at the time. There was probably one of the documents that had arrived from Jablanica that stated "forward command post," and I followed that. I didn't make this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is a forward command post, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each commander from brigade level up, division, Corps, army, and so on and so forth, is entitled to set up a forward command post according to tactical and doctrinal rules. Forward command post? What does that mean? And I'm speaking in general terms. In order to -- the basic command post where you usually have the unit commander, the brigade or corps commander, respectively, and the greatest part of the command of the headquarters in its entirety. The entire staff, all the sectors, the assistant commanders who report to the commander and so on and so forth. Should the need arise, in a specific area under the control of that unit on account of specific ongoing combat operations, whether because there are too many mixed-type units because no good communication lines can be set up or because the -- because of the requirements of the type of combat itself that is going on, in order to be more effective and more successful in carrying out combat tasks, or rather, the specific combat mission that he must carry out within his own area of responsibility, a commander may set up a group to be headed by one of his most experienced and responsible officers. That is, an officer from his own command. Usually, you send a deputy to the forward command post. If not a deputy then a chief. If not a chief then the next officer in line, depending on the level of difficulty of the task that this command post faces. Normally if you have a forward command post you appoint a commander and a number of other officers. When I say a number of other officers, what do I mean? I mean that depending on the nature of the task in hand, the task to be carried out by the forward command post, one appoints one or more officers, if possible, from each of the different command bodies of the unit in question. I believe I have been abundantly clear on this issue. If you need any further clarifications, I'll be glad to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've been extremely helpful with that comprehensive answer. Why would the Supreme Command staff have -- have a forward command post in Jablanica, Donja Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have to object to that one. There is a dispute as to whether what there was in that area was really an IKM -- was really a forward command post or not. The term has been used but the issue has been squarely raised in this case as to whether or not that thing called an IKM is in fact a forward command post and functioning as one. So when my friend asks that question, "Why should the supreme court staff have a forward command post in Jablanica, or Donja Jablanica," the preliminary question is: Did they really have one there at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that is a question put by the Prosecution is within the scope of this document, because the forward command post was mentioned in that document. The only issue is that what is that forward command post mentioned in this document. Is that the General Staff's IKM or not? So I don't think there is any problem for the Prosecution to put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said earlier you weren't making it up when you sent this off to the -- or you said in the order that they should report to the Supreme Command staff's IKM in Donja Jablanica. The question is why would the Supreme Command Staff have an IKM in Donja Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, I must say it would be much more logical to ask General Delic, General Divjak or General Stjepan Siber about this. All these were generals who were in top positions in the Supreme Command Staff, and these people could provide the best answer. You're asking me, as one of their subordinates at the time, including General Sefer Halilovic. I'll try to give you an answer. In 1993, and I believe it will take at least a couple of minutes for me to answer this question, was the most critical year for Bosnia and Herzegovina and its armed forces. There were three enemies, three serious enemies that joined forces in 1993, and tried, in a concerted effort, to coordinate their respective forces to crush Bosnia-Herzegovina, to crush its legitimate government, and to force the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to capitulate. These three enemies were: The Army of the Republic of Srpska; the Army of Yugoslavia led by the Belgrade regime; the next enemy was the Croatian Defence Council, and the Croatian army, led by the regime in Zagreb; the third enemy was Fikret Abdic, himself a product of an agreement between those two other enemies, Milosevic and Tudjman. What was the gist of their agreement back in 1993? And then after that, I would go on to explain the need to set up a forward command post. In 1993, they distributed tasks among themselves. The army of the Republic of Srpska said in 1993, we shall keep conquering parts of the territory under the control of the BH army throughout the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, north to south, or rather from Trebinje to Bijeljina. I assume that each and every one of us are able to imagine the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1993, the Army of the Republika Srpska conquered large chunks of territory in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina thereby turning Gorazde into an enclave, turning Zepa into an enclave, and turning Srebrenica into an enclave. Failing by a narrow margin to place Sarajevo in the second ring. Throughout the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in central Bosnia, around Banja Luka and in the broader area carried out no offensive operations whatsoever, because it had reached an agreement with the Croatian Defence Council that they would carry out a huge amount of offensive operations in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council obliged in the spring of 1993 and launched offensive operations in Central Bosnia covering almost the entire area of responsibilities of the 3rd Corps, including the 4th Corps and including the 6th Corps. The objective of the Croatian Defence Council was to achieve a military occupation of the territory which they considered to be part of their three communities of the Croatian Herceg-Bosna. The first Herceg Bosnia was established on the 18th of November 1991, comprised 30 municipalities. The second one, Bosanska Posavina comprised ten municipalities, and the third one, in Central Bosnia, the central one, comprised four municipalities. When the Supreme Command of Bosnia and Herzegovina felt the blade of a knife at its throat, to be quite literal, it was only then that the 3rd Corps was allowed to go and clash with the Croatian Defence Council. It was only a matter of days before the army would capitulate. The 3rd Corps launched a number of operations and throughout June and July improved their military situation. The Croatian Defence Council experienced a degree of failure in central Bosnia, in military terms, and they realised that there was no way they could achieve their objectives in the summer of 1993. Then they decided to cleanse Herzegovina. They launched an attack on Mostar and the entire Neretva River valley in concert with the Army of the Republic of Srpska. I'm not saying this off the top of my head now. All that I'm saying is based on specific documents. The Neretva operation 93 was planned and was fully justified from a purely military point of view, if you ask me. I'm not talking about crimes. Crimes, of course, were not justified. I am talking about the Neretva 93 operation from a purely military standpoint. Once the Croatian Defence Council had failed to cleanse Central Bosnia, they wanted to make sure they would cleanse Herzegovina, the Neretva River valley, and whatever they managed to conquer. Negotiations in Bosnia-Herzegovina were coming to an end, followed by the Washington Agreement on the Federation. Now we are coming to our old question: Why did one need to set up a forward command post if, indeed, it was a forward command post? I'm not committing myself either way. The reason was, precisely, the complex military problems that were being faced, but we must never forget about the political problems faced at the time. The greatest problem to the military officers of Bosnia-Herzegovina was how to establish some sort of communication with the civilian bodies of government, and also how to establish coordination between the 4th and the 6th corps and part of the 3rd corps. I believe Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf were by this time already within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and the central area around Konjic and the broader area was under the 6th Corps, while Mostar and its surroundings were under the 4th Corps. If you look at this map and realise the extent of the area that this operations plan covered, and I'm speaking from a purely military point of view, it would have been natural to set up a body like that in order to prevent plans devised by the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian army from coming to fruition in Herzegovina. I forgot to mention the third enemy, namely Fikret Abdic. He tried to use his own army to crush the 5th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Bihac area, and in the broader area around Bihac. He failed in his intention to crush the 5th Corps but he managed to take some of their territory and control it for a period of time. This army was led by Fikret Abdic, the self-styled president of the Autonomous Region Bosanska Krajina. He was tried for this in Zagreb after the war and he was sentenced to 20 years of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think we are over time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think it's time for us to adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
